chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and the record business
title: Unpaid for the record, then Granz's tour wages
summary: Hearing himself on a record, he is paid seventy dollars after the union's limit, then paid two hundred and fifty on tour.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I was walking down the street in Los Angeles when I heard me playing. And I said, "What the fuck... I wonder what the hell is this. I know I ain't made no records since I been out here." So I go in the store, and I say, "What is that record you just got through playing?" He said, "Oh, that's the new volume of Jazz at the Philharmonic." I said, "Oh yeah? Who is putting that record out?" Then he told me Asch and Norman Granz. And I said, "Oh yeah?"

So I called Norman, and I said, "Hey, Norman, you put out that record, right?" He said, "Oh yeah, didn't you get your check yet?" I said, "What check?" He said, "Oh, I'll put a check in the mail to you." I said, "You dig?" I said, "Well, now, what is this," you know. So I went to the union, I said, "This man got a record out on me, and I haven't gotten paid for it. He said he's sending me a check." So the guy tells me, he said, "Well, Fain [Elmer Fain] said if he sends you over thirty dollars, that's all we can do." I said, "Yeah? That's all?" He said, "Yeah, that's all we can do." So I said, "Okay, well, if that's what the union says, that's the way it is." So I got a check from Norman; he gave me seventy dollars.
Plus you had gotten paid for the gig

Yeah, that was thirty dollars. So that was a yard I made for the whole thing. So he got straight behind it! And from then on... Well, he considered me a California boy, because that's where I met him, out in California. But I mean, I was really from New York, and I knew more about what was going on than he thought I did.

Anyway, he said, "Look, I want you to make a tour with me." So I said to myself, I know he ain't gonna pay me no money... I knew what he was paying Jacquet and I knew what he was paying the rest of the guys, so I sounded him. I said, "Yeah, well, okay, I don't mind making a tour for you, but I can't go for no California wages." So he said, "Oh no! We wouldn't go in for that. I'll take care of everything." I said, "Oh you will, huh?" "Yeah." So I said, "Yeah, okay."

So when we went out and made the first week, he gave me two-hundred-and-fifty dollars. And I said, "You're just taking care of me. Right?" So he said, "Well, I know you've got more expense out here on the road than you have in California." I said, "But who's thinking about California? I was thinking about me, period." But he wouldn't get up off no money. He wouldn't give me no money, man.
But I remember seeing you in Kansas City... When I was
going to school in the Midwest, we went to Kansas City to see Jazz at the Philharmonic. It was you and Flip Phillips and Bill Harris and Hank Jones...
Yeah, I didn't have nothin' else to do, so what was I gonna do? Turn down two-hundred-fifty dollars? No.
